stories.headline: SpaceX prepared first Starship orbital test from its Texas base
stories.dek: The flight was set to carry 26 Starlink satellites and test fixes after the last booster failed to land safely.
paragraphs: SpaceX was preparing to launch Starship from its Starbase site in Texas in the company’s first attempt to send the giant rocket into orbit. The test matters now because SpaceX wants to prove Starship can carry payloads, survive re-entry, and support future NASA Moon missions.

Starship is the biggest and most powerful rocket SpaceX has built. The company has flown it before, but earlier missions were suborbital tests or ended with failures. On the previous flight, Starship deployed test satellites, but the Super Heavy booster failed to complete a safe landing after engine problems during its return.

It was still unclear whether the launch would go ahead on time, with SpaceX’s website saying regulatory approval was pending. The hardest parts also remained ahead: reaching orbit, releasing 26 Starlink satellites, and bringing both stages back down in a controlled way without another breakup or crash.
stories.changes: If the test works, SpaceX moves closer to using Starship for satellite launches and later crewed Moon missions.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean routine Mars flights are near, and one successful test would not make Starship a proven everyday rocket.

cover.title: SpaceX prepared first Starship orbital test launch in Texas
cover.standfirst: SpaceX was set to launch Starship from Starbase, Texas, on its first attempt to reach orbit. The rocket was due to carry 26 Starlink satellites and test booster landing fixes after the last flight ended with a hard splashdown. Success would help NASA’s Moon plans, but approval and the hardest flight stages still remained.

art.label: Bold symbol
art.concept: Show the actual Starship stacked on the actual Super Heavy in a stark, straight-on ascent from Starbase, centered high enough that the lower third stays mostly open for type. Render the vehicle as one dominant dark silhouette against a flat pale ground, but cut a single jagged off-white vertical void through the stack at the stage-separation point so it first reads as normal separation and then as the rocket tearing open; add only a few tiny debris-like dots drifting from that break, and a minimal suggestion of launch mount at the base so this cannot be mistaken for any other rocket story.
art.note: Tense and clean; steel gray, white vapor, pale blue sky.
art.second_beat: The white cut first reads as successful staging, then a split-second later as a breakup wound—the same shape holding promise and failure at once.

stories.headline: Hurricane Polo nears Baja California Sur as evacuations preparations begin
stories.dek: Officials closed schools, opened shelters and warned of flooding, mudslides and dangerous surf near Los Cabos.
paragraphs: Hurricane Polo is moving toward Mexico’s northern Pacific coast and could reach Baja California Sur late Monday or early Tuesday. Forecasters say the storm has sustained winds near 115 mph. Authorities are preparing now because heavy rain, storm surge and large waves could quickly make roads, beaches and low-lying areas dangerous.

Baja California Sur includes Los Cabos, a major tourist area at the southern tip of the peninsula. Officials have closed schools for Monday, opened temporary shelters and restricted access to beaches in Cabo San Lucas. Residents have been buying water and food, while federal authorities sent thousands of navy and army personnel with specialized equipment.

The exact landfall point and the worst-hit communities are still uncertain. Forecasts also can change in strength before the storm reaches shore. It is not yet clear how many people may need evacuation, how severe flooding or mudslides will be, or how long transport, tourism and local services could be disrupted.
stories.changes: If you live in or travel to Baja California Sur, expect closures, rough seas, possible evacuations and fast-changing weather through Tuesday.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all of Mexico’s Pacific coast will see the same damage, and forecasts can still shift before landfall.

cover.title: Hurricane Polo heads for Baja California Sur in Mexico
cover.standfirst: Hurricane Polo is forecast to reach Baja California Sur late Monday or early Tuesday with winds near 115 mph. Officials closed schools, opened shelters and blocked beach access in Los Cabos as forecasters warned of flooding, mudslides, storm surge and destructive waves.

art.label: Gouache painting
art.concept: Paint one unmistakably Cabo coastal road seen straight-on, running horizontally across the page with the Sea of Cortez on one side and low stucco hotels, palms, and a few parked cars on the other. A diagonal wall of rain sweeps through the same view, turning the left side from dry ochre pavement and calm beach into the right side where the road is already half-submerged, one sawhorse barricade is tipping in the water, and the palms are bent hard inland; keep the lower third mostly simple road and floodwater so type can sit there. Make the Los Cabos setting clear through the resort-strip architecture and desert-coast palette, not signs or words.
art.note: Tense coastal weather, muted blue-gray and sand tones with sharp white surf
art.second_beat: The second beat is that the disaster is not spectacle but access quietly failing—the same ordinary evacuation road becoming unusable in front of you.

stories.headline: Nepal avalanche kills four as rescuers search for 12 missing
stories.dek: The victims were Nepali base camp workers on Mount Himlung preparing for the autumn climbing season.
paragraphs: Rescue teams in northern Nepal were searching Monday for 12 people missing after an avalanche struck Mount Himlung base camp a day earlier. At least four people were killed and 10 were rescued by helicopter. The search continued as severe weather hit the Himalayan country.

Mount Himlung is a 23,380-foot peak in north-central Nepal. The people killed or missing were Nepali nationals working at base camp before foreign climbers arrived for the autumn season, which began this month. Heavy rain also caused flooding and landslides in Manang district over the weekend.

It is still unclear whether the 12 missing people can be reached and how bad conditions remain on the mountain. Officials have not said when the search might end. Nepal is also dealing with wider storm damage after dozens of weather-related deaths across the country in recent days.
stories.changes: For travelers and climbers in Nepal, severe weather is disrupting mountain access and raising the risk around expeditions.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean all climbing in Nepal has stopped, or that every mountain route in the country is affected in the same way.

cover.title: Avalanche on Mount Himlung leaves 12 missing in Nepal
cover.standfirst: An avalanche hit base camp on Mount Himlung in northern Nepal on Sunday, killing at least four Nepali workers and leaving 12 missing. Ten people were flown to safety. Rescuers were still searching Monday as heavy rain, floods and landslides hit the region.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: Engrave the avalanche as a single massive near-black diagonal slab sweeping from upper left to lower right, its surface cut with a few violent white gouges and broken textures of churned snow. Through the center of that black mass, carve a clean cream negative-space silhouette of a rescue helicopter banking inward, unmistakable by rotor disc and tail boom; at the very bottom edge, keep the lower third mostly quiet, with only two or three snapped tent guy-lines and a torn flap of base-camp fabric half-buried in the debris to fix the scale and the camp setting.
art.note: Quiet, cold, and stark; slate gray, snow white, and muted blue.
art.second_beat: First it reads as the avalanche itself; a beat later the empty white cut resolves into the helicopter searching the void left by the missing.

stories.headline: China and the US plan tariff cuts on $60 billion
stories.dek: Both governments published product lists as they try to lower trade friction before more talks.
paragraphs: China and the United States said they will cut tariffs on $60 billion in goods, releasing separate lists that cover thousands of products. The step is meant to ease trade tensions now, before further negotiations, and to give businesses clearer rules for some cross-border trade.

Tariffs are taxes paid on imported goods. In recent years, the two countries raised them during a long trade fight that disrupted supply chains and raised costs for companies buying parts, materials and finished products. Those costs can then spread through factories, wholesalers, retailers and consumers.

It is not yet clear which products will see the biggest changes, how deep the cuts will be across all categories, or when every change takes effect. Bigger disputes between the two governments also remain. More talks are expected, so this looks like a limited easing, not a full settlement.
stories.changes: Some importers and manufacturers may soon pay less on listed goods, which can lower costs and reduce delays in planning orders.
stories.unchanged: This does not end the wider US-China trade dispute, and it does not mean prices will quickly fall across the whole economy.

cover.title: China and the United States plan tariff cuts on goods
cover.standfirst: China and the United States said they will cut tariffs on $60 billion in goods and published lists covering thousands of products. The move is meant to cool trade tensions before more negotiations, but the wider dispute between the two countries is not settled.

art.label: Drawn chart
art.concept: Fill the upper two-thirds with a dense field of thick, hand-drawn vertical tariff bars, all nearly identical in dark ink, reading at first glance as a hard wall. Cut one clear path through that wall with the silhouette of a container ship moving sideways across the bars: as it passes, it shaves a single central bar down to a shorter accent-colour stub, with a few clipped fragments flying off the cut. Keep the lower third mostly open and quiet for type, with only the ship’s hull just entering that space so the action is unmistakably trade, not abstract finance.
art.note: Clear, sober, economic; muted blues, red accents, off-white background.
art.second_beat: First you see a chart-wall being cut by a ship; a beat later you realise only one bar has been reduced, so the tariff relief is narrow inside a much larger regime that still stands.

stories.headline: Russian drone strike sets Kyiv academy building on fire
stories.dek: A woman was killed and emergency crews worked through heavy smoke at a National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv.
paragraphs: A Russian drone attack hit central Kyiv on Sept. 28 and set a National Academy of Sciences building on fire in the Shevchenkivskyi district. Video showed flames and thick smoke around the three-story building. City officials said at least one woman was killed as crews responded.

The strike was part of a wider attack on Kyiv overnight and into the day. Authorities also reported damage in the Podilskyi, Holosiivskyi, Darnytskyi and Obolonskyi districts. Gas stations and other nonresidential buildings were damaged. Kyiv has faced repeated Russian drone and missile attacks throughout the war.

Officials had not yet given a full casualty count or explained how many people were inside the academy building when it was hit. The extent of damage to the scientific institution was also unclear. Investigators still need to confirm the exact weapon used and the full path of the attack.
stories.changes: For Kyiv residents, this means another day of disrupted streets, emergency closures, and renewed risk even in central districts.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Kyiv's air defenses have collapsed or that every public building in the city is now unusable.

cover.title: Russian drone strike sets Kyiv science building on fire
cover.standfirst: A Russian drone attack on Sept. 28 hit a National Academy of Sciences building in central Kyiv, causing a large fire and heavy smoke. City officials said a woman was killed, and damage was also reported in four other districts as emergency crews worked at the scene.

art.label: Engraving
art.concept: Inside the National Academy of Sciences, show a polished institutional corridor in steep perspective, its far end completely swallowed by a dense wall of smoke. A fire hose snakes in from the lower edge, across the floor and into the smoke; beside it, unmistakably scientific debris has just been knocked down — a tipped microscope slide rack with dozens of thin glass slides scattered across wet tiles, the first dark water from the hose reaching them. Keep the lower third spare: hose, tiles, slides, water, with the smoke mass and corridor architecture carrying the upper frame.
art.note: Somber and quiet; ash gray, smoke black, muted orange.
art.second_beat: First you see firefighters pushing into smoke; a beat later you notice the water washing over microscope slides, and the loss resolves from fire damage into interrupted scientific work at a painfully small scale.

stories.headline: Three migrants die in Channel crossing crush off northern France
stories.dek: French rescuers pulled 105 people from an inflatable boat after a distress call, but a 10-year-old child and two women died.
paragraphs: Three migrants died on Monday during an attempted English Channel crossing from northern France. French authorities said a 10-year-old child and two women were on an inflatable dinghy carrying 105 people when rescuers were called. Officials said the likely cause of death was crushing, not drowning.

The boat had left Bleriot Plage near Calais on Monday morning. A helicopter brought a medical team to the rescue vessel, but the three could not be saved. The Channel route remains one of the main paths used by people trying to reach Britain from France in small, overloaded boats.

It is not yet clear exactly how the crushing happened on board or where passengers were positioned when the emergency began. French authorities are still investigating the deaths. The case is also likely to add pressure on British and French officials already facing scrutiny over small-boat crossings and border enforcement.
stories.changes: For readers, this is another sign that Channel crossings can turn deadly even before a boat sinks.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean Channel crossings have stopped or that every rescue call ends in deaths.

cover.title: Three migrants die in crush on Channel crossing boat
cover.standfirst: French rescuers pulled 105 people from an inflatable dinghy off Pas-de-Calais on Monday after a distress call. A 10-year-old child and two women died, with officials saying the likely cause was crushing. Authorities are investigating how it happened on board.

art.label: Punk cutout
art.concept: On a hazard-orange ground, show one continuous overhead Channel dinghy running vertically through the page so it reads as the same boat changing state. At the top edge, it has just pushed off from a blunt black strip of northern French beach; by the middle it is visibly overloaded with dense black cutout heads packed inside; by the lower half the oval has pinched inward into a cramped waist as thick black rescue-gloved hands enter from both sides, compressing the crowd into a knot. Keep the bottom third mostly open orange, with only the lower part of the distorted boat and a few hands crossing into it, so type can sit cleanly over the field.
art.second_beat: First you see a crossing route; a beat later you realise the same dinghy is transforming from departure into a fatal crush, so the disaster is compression, not simply sinking.

stories.headline: Kremlin warns Ukraine will pay after strikes inside Russia
stories.dek: Moscow said its military campaign will continue and also urged quick new arms control talks with the United States.
paragraphs: The Kremlin said Ukraine will pay a price for recent strikes on Russian territory. Spokesman Dmitry Peskov said Russian military operations would continue. The warning came as Moscow reacted to attacks it says crossed deeper into Russia and raised pressure on its security forces.

Russia and Ukraine have been at war since Russia's full-scale invasion in 2022. Since then, fighting has spread beyond the front line through missile attacks, drone strikes and cross-border raids. Moscow also said urgent arms control talks with the United States should restart despite the wider breakdown in relations.

It is not yet clear what response Russia is preparing or whether the warning points to immediate new attacks. There is also no sign of when arms control talks might resume, what weapons they would cover, or whether Washington is willing to engage now.
stories.changes: For ordinary readers, this signals a risk of more Russian military action and another rise in tension between Moscow and Washington.
stories.unchanged: It does not mean a new war has started, and it does not by itself show any change in the front lines.

cover.title: Kremlin says Ukraine will pay for strikes inside Russia
cover.standfirst: The Kremlin said Ukraine will face consequences after strikes on Russian territory and said Russian military operations will continue. Moscow also called for urgent new arms control talks with the United States, though there is no clear sign yet of when talks could begin.

art.label: Silkscreen
art.concept: A single matryoshka doll, unmistakably Russian in silhouette and pattern, is split into two vertical halves against an otherwise empty field. On the left, the opened shell reveals the expected smaller doll, calm and centred; on the right, the same shell has just sprung apart and a small attack drone is dropping out nose-first, caught mid-fall into a quiet lower third. Keep it to black and off-register signal red only, with a few tiny red flecks at the split seam so the opening reads at once as cracked lacquer, impact and alarm breaking loose from inside Russia.
art.note: Severe and spare; black, deep red and ash grey.
art.second_beat: First you read a familiar Russian nesting doll; a beat later you realise the thing inside is not another doll but an attack drone, making the threat feel home-grown and newly released from within Russia itself.

stories.headline: Oil rises more than 4 percent after Trump rejects Iran offer
stories.dek: Brent crude climbed above $108 a barrel after Trump said no to Iran's proposal to reopen the Strait of Hormuz.
paragraphs: Oil prices rose sharply on Monday after Donald Trump rejected an Iranian proposal tied to reopening the Strait of Hormuz. Brent crude climbed more than 4% to $108.48 a barrel, while U.S. crude reached $96.16. Traders reacted because the offer had raised hopes of easing a major supply risk.

The Strait of Hormuz is a narrow sea route used to ship a large share of the world's oil. Iran had said it could reopen the passage and restart nuclear talks within seven days if Washington met several demands, including ending military pressure, lifting the naval blockade and releasing Iranian assets.

What happens next depends on whether the United States and Iran return to talks or move back toward open conflict. Traders are also watching for any disruption in Gulf shipping and for signs that oil stockpiles are being drawn down further. Fuel prices could stay volatile for now.
stories.changes: This raises the risk of higher petrol, diesel and heating costs if oil stays elevated.
stories.unchanged: There is no immediate physical supply cutoff, and pump prices will not jump everywhere at once today.

cover.title: Oil jumps after Trump rejects Iran plan to reopen strait
cover.standfirst: Brent crude rose more than 4% to $108.48 a barrel on Monday after Donald Trump rejected Iran's offer to reopen the Strait of Hormuz. Tehran had linked the route's reopening and new nuclear talks to U.S. concessions. Traders now see a higher risk of renewed conflict and tighter oil supply.

art.label: Drawn chart
art.concept: Make the cover a blunt rising bar chart spanning the upper half of the page, with the bars stepping sharply upward from left to right. In the middle, the white gap between two tall bars must clearly resolve into the narrow pinch of the Strait of Hormuz, and at the far right one final bar in the accent colour jumps abruptly higher, as if the squeeze has just tightened and sent prices surging. Keep the lower third almost entirely empty for type.
art.note: Tense and spare, with deep blue sea, black lines, and a sharp red price surge.
art.second_beat: First it reads as a price chart; a beat later the gaps become the Strait itself, so the market rise is caused by the chokepoint closing.

stories.headline: Serbia's president resigns to seek power again as prime minister
stories.dek: Aleksandar Vucic quit the presidency before an early parliamentary election after months of pressure from protests against his rule.
paragraphs: Serbian President Aleksandar Vucic resigned on Sunday so he can run for prime minister in an early parliamentary election. The vote will test whether he can keep his grip on power after nearly two years of protests. By stepping down now, he shifts the political fight from the presidency to parliament.

Vucic has dominated Serbian politics for years and is widely described as a populist leader. Serbia has faced long-running street protests from opponents angry about his style of rule and the state of public life. An early election turns that unrest into a direct contest over who will control the government.

It is still unclear when the election will be held, who will replace Vucic as president in the meantime, and whether his allies can win enough seats to keep governing. It is also not clear whether the opposition can unite strongly enough to turn protest energy into votes.
stories.changes: Serbians now face an election that could decide whether the same leader keeps power from a different office.
stories.unchanged: This does not mean Vucic is leaving politics or that Serbia's direction will change immediately.

cover.title: Serbia's president resigns to run for prime minister
cover.standfirst: Aleksandar Vucic resigned as Serbia's president on Sunday and will seek the prime minister's job in an early parliamentary election. The vote follows nearly two years of protests over his rule. The result will show whether he can keep control through parliament instead of the presidency.

art.label: Object photograph
art.concept: On a clean field in muted Serbian tricolour tones, show a polished wooden presidential desk nameplate holder alone, shot straight-on and low enough that the lower third stays mostly empty. Where the metal plaque should be, a folded, unmistakably ballot-like parliamentary paper is being pushed halfway out of the slot mid-motion, curling downward under its own weight like a tongue; keep everything else out of frame so the holder itself appears to be ejecting its next office.
art.note: Tense but orderly; muted reds, cream, and charcoal.
art.second_beat: First you see a formal presidential object misbehaving; a beat later you realise the presidency is not ending but spitting itself directly into parliament.

stories.headline: Sweden deadlock deepens after Andersson drops coalition bid
stories.dek: The center-left bloc won 176 of 349 seats, but two allied parties would not serve together.
paragraphs: Sweden's bid for a new government stalled on Monday when Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson said coalition talks had failed. Her center-left bloc won the election by a narrow margin, but she could not unite four parties behind one cabinet because internal disputes remained unresolved.

The Social Democrats, Greens, Center Party and Left Party together hold 176 seats in Sweden's 349-seat parliament. The outgoing right-wing alliance has 173. The split is small, and the popular vote gap was about 50,000. Sweden often needs broad deals because no bloc can govern alone.

Parliament's speaker is expected to ask another leader to try next, likely outgoing Prime Minister Ulf Kristersson. He also lacks a majority. The Center Party says it will not back a government that depends on either the far-right Sweden Democrats or the Left Party.
stories.changes: Sweden may spend longer under a caretaker government while party leaders test new deals.
stories.unchanged: The election result stands, and day-to-day government services continue while talks drag on.

cover.title: Sweden coalition talks collapse after election leaves split parliament
cover.standfirst: Social Democratic leader Magdalena Andersson said she could not form a government after talks between four center-left parties broke down in Stockholm. Her bloc won 176 of 349 seats on September 13, but deep splits remain. Parliament's speaker is now expected to ask another leader, likely Ulf Kristersson, to try.

art.label: Cut mosaic
art.concept: Inside the unmistakable green-and-gold horseshoe of the Riksdag chamber, a bright yellow Swedish ballot is being lowered straight down like a fitted insert. It should slot neatly into the chamber, but it jams halfway because two clean bite-shaped notches missing from opposite edges stop it from seating; at the point of impact, a few mosaic seat-tiles crack and kick outward, while the lower third stays mostly dark and clear for type.
art.note: Cool civic mood, muted blues and greens with one sharp contrasting accent.
art.second_beat: First you see a government that will not fit into parliament; then you realise the blockage is caused by two absences—the allied parties that refuse to sit together.
